label: exercise
title: Exercise: a cloud API gateway flaw may have exposed every secret stored in it
real_story: Norway's NSM says an unknown actor has actively gone after access tokens, secrets and named values in Azure API Management (APIM), and names Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the organisations affected. Microsoft says it found the vulnerability on November 18, 2026 and patched it the next day. It says an unauthorized party could have used the issue to reach secrets in Classic instances that were not configured to its security guidelines. Microsoft says the fix does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been used earlier. NSM tells every APIM user to assume their secrets and named values may be exposed and to rotate all tokens and secrets.

facts.text: NSM says an unknown actor has actively targeted access tokens, secrets and named values in APIM.
NSM says Equinor and Skagerak Energi are among the organisations that have been affected.
NSM says everyone using Azure API Management should assume their secrets and named values may be compromised, and that organisations must rotate all tokens and secrets.
NSM says an organisation whose instance has not been updated should contact its supplier directly, and one that sees or confirms a compromise should contact NSM.
Microsoft says it found the vulnerability on November 18, 2026 and patched it the next day.
Microsoft says the affected tiers are Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium of APIM Classic; it says the Consumption tier of Classic and all v2 tiers were unaffected.

Microsoft says the fix does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been used before it, and urges customers to change potentially compromised credentials, monitor systems reachable with them and review logs.

The Register reports that exposure was linked to Classic configurations that did not follow Microsoft's network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM instead of referencing Azure Key Vault.

scenario: Hypothetical: Northwind Freight, a 900-person logistics company, runs a classic-tier API gateway in its cloud tenant that fronts customer tracking APIs and partner integrations. Over the years teams stored subscription keys, identity-provider client secrets and backend tokens directly in the gateway; nobody owns a full inventory, and two old test instances still exist. On Monday morning the national cyber agency publishes a warning that a cloud provider flaw let an unknown actor read secrets in such gateways. The provider says it has already fixed the service, but earlier credentials are not automatically invalidated. Your security lead must decide what to assume and what to do first.

injects.title: Agency warning lands
injects.text: A national cyber agency notice says an unknown actor has been going after tokens, secrets and named values in a cloud API gateway. The vendor says the flaw is fixed on its side.
injects.ask: Who owns this? What do you check in the first 15 minutes?

injects.title: Inventory turns up surprises
injects.text: Engineering finds four gateway instances, including two forgotten test instances. Two are classic tier. Several hold secrets directly instead of referencing a key vault.
injects.ask: How do you decide what is in scope, and who confirms the tier and configuration of each?

injects.title: Suspicious admin activity
injects.text: Logs on the production gateway show administrative operations from an unfamiliar address two days before the vendor fix. Retention on the test instances is only 7 days.
injects.ask: Do you declare an incident? What evidence do you preserve now?

injects.title: Partner and media pressure
injects.text: A large partner asks whether its integration keys were exposed. A trade journalist asks if the company is among those affected.
injects.ask: What do you tell the partner and the journalist, and who approves it?

injects.title: Hard decision: rotate everything
injects.text: Rotating all secrets will break customer tracking and three partner integrations for several hours. The executive sponsor asks whether rotation can wait until the weekend.
injects.ask: Decide: rotate now, in stages, or wait? What is your order and your rollback?

injects.title: Recovery and follow-up
injects.text: Rotation is done. A backend service still accepts an old token nobody knew about.
injects.ask: How do you confirm old credentials are dead, and what changes so secrets are not stored in the gateway again?

questions: Who in the organisation can say, within an hour, which cloud API gateways exist, their tier and who owns them?
What would you assume about secrets stored in the gateway, given the vendor says the fix does not invalidate earlier credentials?
In what order would you rotate tokens, client secrets and subscription keys, and what breaks?
Which logs would you review, how far back, and how long are they kept?
How would you find forgotten development and test instances?
What do you tell partners whose keys passed through the gateway, and when?
When would you contact the national cyber agency or a regulator, and who decides?
How do you prove after rotation that old credentials no longer work?
Which systems reachable with the exposed credentials need extra monitoring, and for how long?
What design change would stop secrets living directly in the gateway?
good_looks_like: The team assumes secrets stored in the affected service may be exposed, as NSM advises, instead of waiting for proof.
All tokens and secrets are rotated, with an agreed order and a rollback plan.
Every gateway instance is found, including development and test ones, and its tier and patch status are checked.
Logs are reviewed and preserved before they roll off.
Systems reachable with the exposed credentials are monitored for suspicious activity.
Unpatched or unclear instances are raised with the supplier, and a confirmed compromise is reported to the national agency.
One person owns communications to partners and press and the wording is approved before sending.
Follow-up moves secrets to a managed key vault reference with named owners.
adapt: Small team: drop the partner and media injects, merge roles (one person plays cloud and identity), and focus on inventory and rotation order. Larger or regulated sector (energy, finance): add a regulator-notification inject with a deadline and a supplier-contract question. Not on that cloud provider: swap in any gateway or secrets store that holds credentials for many services.
